summary: Describes how Ethernet VPNs can answer ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery requests on behalf of hosts, using the ARP/ND Extended Community. This cuts the flooding that these requests cause in large broadcast domains, such as at Internet Exchange Points and data centers. It updates the EVPN specification with fuller operational documentation.

eli5.summary: Rather than shouting across a big room asking who has a name, a helper who already knows answers for them.

subtitle: How EVPN edge routers answer ARP and IPv6 neighbor requests themselves instead of flooding them across a huge network.

tldr.problem: In very large broadcast domains, such as Internet Exchange Point peering networks and data centers, every ARP Request and IPv6 Neighbor Solicitation is flooded to every router and host. That load can exhaust the slow-path processors of routers.
tldr.mechanism: Each EVPN Provider Edge (PE) keeps a per-domain table of IP-to-MAC bindings (learned by snooping, configured statically, or learned from EVPN routes). It intercepts requests, replies from the table when it can, and floods only when it cannot.
tldr.outcome: Flooding is reduced and can even be suppressed completely when all bindings are provisioned. The RFC also adds duplicate IP detection against ARP/ND spoofing. It updates RFC 7432.

today: RFC 9161 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2022 that updates RFC 7432, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the ARP/ND Extended Community of RFC 9047.

sections.title: The Flooding Problem
sections.content:
RFC 7432 lets an EVPN PE advertise IP-to-MAC pairs it has learned in MAC/IP Advertisement routes (also called RT2). Remote PEs in the same Broadcast Domain (BD) can load those pairs into a Proxy ARP/ND table and answer local ARP Requests or Neighbor Solicitations (NS) themselves, or forward them directly to the owner. This document describes that function in full, together with the ARP/ND Extended Community from RFC 9047, and so updates RFC 7432.

Two settings motivate it. In a data center, ARP Requests use broadcast MAC addresses, so every tenant system in a large domain sees traffic not meant for it. Some implementations also keep retrying requests for hosts that have disappeared, as RFC 6820 notes. At an Internet Exchange Point (IXP), hundreds of routers share one Layer 2 domain, and most broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast traffic is ARP and ND. Because routers handle these messages in slow-path software at high priority, heavy loads can leave a router unable to keep its BGP sessions running. The amount of flooded traffic grows linearly with the number of participants.

sections.title: How Proxy ARP/ND Works
sections.content:
When Proxy ARP/ND is turned on in a BD, each PE builds a proxy table for that BD with three kinds of entries: dynamic (learned by snooping a customer edge device's ARP and ND messages), static (provisioned by the management system) and EVPN-learned (taken from RT2 routes sent by remote PEs).

When a customer edge (CE) device sends an ARP Request or NS, its PE intercepts it and looks up the target IP. If the lookup succeeds, the PE sends the ARP Reply or Neighbor Advertisement (NA) itself, and the request is not flooded to the EVPN network or to other local CEs. If it fails, the PE floods the request as usual. The same logic applies to IPv4 and IPv6, with differences in how entries are learned.

As the table fills, flooding between PEs shrinks. Where CEs do not move and announce themselves with gratuitous ARP or unsolicited NA messages, it can practically be suppressed, and in an IXP where all entries are static it is totally suppressed. The RFC splits the function into six sub-functions: learning, reply, unicast-forward, maintenance, flood handling and duplicate IP detection. An implementation MUST support at least learning, reply, maintenance and duplicate IP detection.

sections.title: Learning Entries and the NA Flags
sections.content:
A PE MUST support dynamic and EVPN-learned entries and SHOULD support static ones. A static entry that is advertised in EVPN MUST carry the ARP/ND Extended Community with the Immutable ARP/ND Binding flag (I) set to 1, which says the IP must not be tied to any other MAC. A static entry may list several allowed MACs for one IP; the PE advertises only the one it actually sees traffic from. If a static entry has the same IP as a dynamic or EVPN-learned one, the static entry wins.

For IPv4, a PE MUST snoop all ARP packets (Ethertype 0x0806) from attached CEs, but not those from remote PEs, and learn the sender MAC and IP. For IPv6, it MUST snoop NA messages (ICMPv6 type 136) and MUST NOT learn from NS messages, because an NS lacks the Router (R) flag that the reply function needs.

The R and Override (O) flags are stored with each entry, learned from snooped NAs, from the ARP/ND Extended Community or from configuration, with a default of 1. An optional IPv6 anycast capability lets an IP map to several MACs by learning entries with O = 0; when it is on, duplicate IP detection must be disabled.

After a PE reboot, static and EVPN entries return once the routes arrive, but dynamic entries are gone and are relearned gradually as requests are flooded.

sections.title: Replying and Unicast-Forwarding
sections.content:
On a table hit, the PE SHOULD use the entry's MAC as the Ethernet source address, so switches between the PE and the CE can learn it. An ARP reply MUST carry the entry's IP and MAC as sender addresses; an NA MUST use the entry's IP as source and Target Address and the MAC as the Target Link Layer Address. A PE SHOULD NOT reply when the request arrived on the same attachment circuit where the entry was learned, since the owner already hears it. It SHOULD reply to broadcast or multicast requests (ARP Requests, ARP probes, NS and DAD NS) and SHOULD NOT reply to unicast ones such as NUD NS messages.

For Proxy ND, a PE MUST answer NS messages with known options as RFC 4861 defines them. For unknown options an operator may choose reply, discard, unicast-forward or forward; forward, which floods based on the destination MAC, is the recommended choice.

The unicast-forward sub-function (RECOMMENDED) sends a matching request straight to the owner's MAC instead of replying. With always it does this for every hit, keeping the domain transparent while cutting flooding. With unknown-options it does so only for requests carrying unknown options. With no table hit, the request is flooded.

sections.title: Aging, Refreshing and Flood Control
sections.content:
Dynamic entries MUST be flushed, and their RT2 withdrawn, if they are not refreshed within an administrative age-time. The RFC suggests a longer age-time in IXPs, where routers are fairly static, than in data centers, where hosts move. A PE MAY also send periodic refresh probes to the owners of dynamic entries so they are refreshed before they age out; the recommended timer is a third of the age-time, or a half in scaled networks. Probes go only to the attachment circuit of the entry's MAC, and only for dynamic entries. If the owner replies, both the bridge-table and proxy entries are reset and an unnecessary EVPN withdrawal is avoided.

Flood handling lets an operator choose whether to suppress flooding to remote PEs of unknown requests and of gratuitous ARP and unsolicited NA messages. In an IXP with all entries provisioned, suppression can be total. If a PE might not learn all local entries, flooding SHOULD NOT be suppressed, or some resolutions will never complete. Where fast mobility is expected, as in data centers, suppression is NOT RECOMMENDED.

sections.title: Duplicate IP Detection
sections.content:
A Proxy ARP/ND implementation MUST support duplicate IP detection so spoofing attacks, or plain human error, can be caught. IPv6 hosts still run Duplicate Address Detection (RFC 4862); this is an extra check by the PEs. RFC 6957 is not suitable here because it assumes split-horizon topologies.

When an active IP-to-MAC entry changes, the PE starts an M-second timer (default 180) and counts IP moves; reaching N moves before it expires means a duplicate. Static entries, including EVPN entries with I = 1, are exempt and MUST NOT be overridden by dynamic ones. To detect faster, the PE SHOULD send a unicast Confirm message to the former owner; the recommended wait is 30 seconds. If both the legitimate owner and a spoofer keep answering, the duplicate is detected.

Once detected, the entry cannot be updated by dynamic or EVPN-learned entries (an operator may override it with a static one), and the PE SHOULD alert the operator and stop answering for that IP. Optionally it may bind the IP to an anti-spoofing MAC (AS-MAC), announced by gratuitous ARP or unsolicited NA and an RT2, so that CEs send traffic for that IP to a MAC PEs can drop or log. The condition clears on operator action or after a hold-down timer (default 540 seconds). For Proxy ND, only moves learned from NAs with O = 1 are monitored.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC describes four levels of control. All dynamic learning turns Proxy ARP/ND off, so requests flood as in VPLS. Dynamic learning with Proxy ARP/ND snoops, replies and floods only on a miss. A hybrid adds static entries for protected hosts such as management and infrastructure systems. All static provisioning disables snooping, discards requests for unknown IPs at the ingress PE and gives the operator full control.

IXPs mostly use all static provisioning, which fits their port-security rules, and are advised to configure the reply function to discard requests with unrecognized options. The RFC walks through an IXP customer life cycle: allowlisting the router's MAC and adding static IP-to-MAC entries, adding the new MAC before a router replacement, and removing entries on decommissioning. Data centers prefer dynamic or hybrid models because of mobility, may need IPv6 anycast (which disables duplicate IP detection) and may need to forward or discard unknown options.
sections.eli5: Some places let the helper learn names by listening, some give it a fixed list, and busy exchanges that never change use only the fixed list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7432 and RFC 9047 apply, and EVPN itself provides no cryptographic protection or confidentiality. Cutting flooding protects the slow-path processors of routers and tenant systems, and suppressing unknown requests adds protection against requests for non-existing hosts. The cost is risk: unicast-forward and flood suppression can block a CE if the PEs cannot provide the resolution it needs.

Duplicate IP detection and the AS-MAC guard against ARP/ND spoofing and the denial-of-service attacks that start with it. When anycast is enabled, the operator MUST limit how many entries one IP may have, to stop a flood of entries filling the table. IXPs must still follow established best practices, such as disabling unneeded control protocols and permitting only IPv4, ARP and IPv6 Ethertypes. Finally, the solution will not work if CEs secure their own ARP/ND exchanges, because the PE cannot secure the proxied messages.
